titleSource: Dodging Bullets: Fear-Setting and Escaping Paralysis

sittings.bodyEn: Most people vote no on a jump, brave or not, because uncertainty sounds worse than a familiar unhappy life. Years of goals can die in that gap. The move in this chapter is to stop calling the fog a mood and to write the nightmare in concrete scenes. Vague dread is what keeps the trip, the quit, or the ask imaginary. Once the worst case is a list, the repair steps usually look ordinary, and the freeze loses its best trick. Fear-setting is that list, done on paper, before you decide.

terms.hook: Writing the nightmare, the repair, and the likely upside so a decision can move.
The story that a dull path will improve by itself, used to avoid a jump.

sittings.bodyEn: Set aside the polish and write the absolute worst that could follow the change you are considering. Include the doubts, the fears, and the what-ifs, and describe them in detail instead of in a headline. Ask whether it would end your life. Score any permanent impact from one to ten, then ask whether those outcomes are actually permanent. Write how likely you think each one is. Spend a few minutes, aim for volume, and do not edit while you pour it out. Thinking harder in your head is the stall this page is replacing.

terms.hook: The concrete worst case of the change, scored for permanence and likelihood.

sittings.bodyEn: Under the nightmare, write the steps that would repair the damage or turn things upward, even for a while. The chapter's claim is that this list is easier than the dread suggested. Ask how you would get the situation back under control. A temporary job, a cut in spending, or a sale of something you do not need can belong on the page. The point is a path back, not a heroic one. If the old life is still available with a bit of extra work, say that in a sentence you can reread when the fear returns.

After the nightmare, write the more probable outcomes, both the ones that pass and the ones that last. Include internal results, such as confidence, and external results, such as a change in how you spend the week. Score the impact of those likelier outcomes from one to ten. Ask how likely a decent result is, even if it is not the dream version. Ask whether people with less talent have already done a version of this and landed it. The comparison the chapter wants is an unlikely, temporary dent against a probable, lasting gain. If the dent is repairable and the gain is large, the page has done its job.

Run the same three pages for a forced case: you are fired today, and you need the money under control. Write that nightmare, the repair, and the probable upside as if the job had already ended. Then answer a second version: you quit in order to test other options, and you later need the old career back. Name the steps that would put you on that track again. This is how the chapter removes the fantasy that leaving is a cliff with no path up. A pause can be indefinite without being a deletion of the old skill.

The action you are postponing out of fear is usually the action you most need. It might be a call or a conversation. Unknown outcomes are what freeze it, so define the worst case, accept that case, and do the thing. Treat that claim as a habit, so the scary action becomes the assignment rather than a mood. A useful score is how many uneasy conversations you will start. Each day, complete one action you have been avoiding because it scares you. The practice in the chapter began with asking well-known people for advice, which made the discomfort a daily rep.

Do not only price the downside of action. Price what the delay costs in money, in feeling, and in your body. If you skip the things that excite you, write where you are in one year, in five years, and in ten. Write how it will feel to have let circumstance choose, and to have spent another decade on work you already know will not fulfill you. If a ten-year look shows disappointment with certainty, the wait is the danger. This chapter treats risk as the chance of a bad result you cannot undo. On that definition, staying put is the danger that dwarfs the rest.

terms.hook: The chance of a harm you cannot undo, which makes waiting the large danger.

sittings.bodyEn: Fear often wears a smarter name, and the common costume is optimism. A boring or uninspiring job, short of pure hell, invites the thought that time or a raise will fix it. Pure hell forces a move, and anything milder can be endured with a clever reason. If you truly expected improvement, you would not be questioning the path this hard. Compare yourself with a year ago, a month ago, and a week ago. If you are not better, the situation will not repair itself, and it is time to plan the jump. A working life of four or five decades is on the order of five hundred months, which is long enough for a rescue that never comes.

The worked example is a miserable stretch of high income, a company that seemed unsellable, and a dream of a year away that sat untouched for six months of shame. Writing the nightmare, including a failed business, a lawsuit, spoiled stock, and a much smaller account, made the trip less frightening. The repair was ordinary: a temporary job if rent demanded it, fewer meals out, and a return to the old grind with extra effort. On a scale from one to ten, that one-in-a-million disaster looked like a temporary three or four. A probable good case looked like a lasting nine or ten. The trade was an unlikely, repairable dent for a probable, permanent change, and the old life was still available. A one-way ticket followed, the disasters did not, and the business funded about fifteen months away while doing better than before.

One lawyer in the chapter dreaded forty more years of the same mornings, slept under a desk, and still needed a physical risk before the resignation became real. After he jumped, the fear of turbulence eased, because the thing he had been protecting was no longer trapped in the job. He could have returned to the old track, and the pause was not a surrender of the degree. A separate account is a volunteer who arrived in a drought, a coup, and a diet of corn meal and greens. After two weeks, the worst was friends plus enough food, and the lesson was that control of time mattered more than luxuries. Both stories are there to make the scores on your page believable: most nightmares are reversible, and the serious loss is the decade you do not spend.

Tonight, answer all seven prompts on paper, a few minutes each, with volume and without editing. The nightmare, the repair, and the likely upside come first, with scores and odds. Then the fired-today page and the path back onto the old track. Then the single feared action, the cost of waiting at one year, five years, and ten, and the sentence about what you are still waiting for. If that last answer sneaks back to good timing, the chapter says you are afraid, like everyone else. Measure the cost of inaction, note how repairable most missteps are, and do one feared action before the page goes cold. The habit to build is action, and the page is only useful if it produces one.

Fear-setting replaces a vague no with a written nightmare, a repair plan, and a scored upside. The scale compares an unlikely temporary dent with a probable lasting gain. A separate page prices the cost of waiting, and this chapter calls inaction the largest risk when the bad outcome would be irreversible. Optimistic stories about a dull job improving on its own are treated as fear in a nicer coat. The daily rep is one uncomfortable action, after the worst case has been accepted. A pause can leave the old career available, which is why the cliff is usually drawn taller than it is.

Write the nightmare and the repair, score the likely upside, price the wait, and do one feared action
Quit first, and write the plan only after the money runs out
